◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real Analysis rebuilds calculus on solid ground. The single property that separates ℝ from ℚ — and makes limits, continuity, and integrals work — is completeness: every bounded set has a least upper bound.

Supremum
The supremum (least upper bound) sup S is the smallest number ≥ every element of S. It need not be IN S. The infimum inf S is the greatest lower bound.
Completeness axiom
Every nonempty subset of ℝ that is bounded above has a supremum in ℝ. (This fails in ℚ: {x : x² < 2} has no rational supremum.)
WORKED EXAMPLE — sup vs max

Let S = {1 − 1/n : n ∈ ℕ} = {0, 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, ...}.

Every element is < 1, and no smaller bound works, so sup S = 1. But 1 ∉ S, so S has NO maximum.

inf S = 0, and since 0 ∈ S (n=1), 0 is also the minimum.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

sup S is not always achieved. A maximum is a supremum that happens to belong to the set; a set can have a sup without a max.

📊 FIGURE — Supremum on the number line
S = (0, 1) is bounded above by 1, 1.5, 2, … — the shaded ray is ALL its upper bounds. The supremum is the least of them: 1. Note 1 ∉ S: a supremum need not belong to the set, which is exactly why \"least upper bound\" is the right notion, not \"maximum\".

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Convergence of sequences is the prototype for every limit in analysis. The ε–N definition makes 'approaches' precise: you name a tolerance ε, and eventually all terms stay within it.

Convergence
aₙ → L means: for every ε > 0 there exists N such that n > N implies |aₙ − L| < ε. The limit is unique when it exists.
WORKED EXAMPLE — proving a limit

Show 1/n → 0.

Given ε > 0, we need |1/n − 0| = 1/n < ε, i.e. n > 1/ε.

Choose N = ⌈1/ε⌉. Then n > N ⇒ 1/n < ε. Since ε was arbitrary, 1/n → 0. ∎

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

N is allowed to DEPEND on ε — smaller ε generally needs larger N. The definition demands 'for every ε, THERE EXISTS an N', not one N for all ε.

📊 FIGURE — Convergence: the sequence enters the ε-band and stays
Pick ANY tolerance ε around L (dashed band). Convergence means: beyond some index N, every term lives inside the band — forever. Early terms may wander freely (they do here); only the tail matters. Shrink ε and a larger N is demanded, but one always exists.
📊 FIGURE — turning the definition into a number
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Finding the smallest N for a given ε

For aₙ = 1/n, L = 0 and ε = 0.001, the requirement |1/n − 0| < 0.001 means

1/n < 1/1000  ⟺  n > 1000

So N = 1000: every n > 1000 satisfies the inequality.

Why not N = 999? Because n = 1000 would then be included, and there 1/1000 = 0.001 exactly — which is not strictly less than ε. The strict inequality is doing real work, and this off-by-one is the whole content of the question.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Alternating signs do not obstruct convergence

For aₙ = (−1)ⁿ/n the terms oscillate: −1, +1/2, −1/3, +1/4, … Yet

|aₙ − 0| = |(−1)ⁿ|/n = 1/n

which is below ε as soon as n > 1/ε. So the ε–N definition is satisfied with L = 0.

The definition only ever looks at the magnitude |aₙ − L|. Alternating signs matter for whether a series converges absolutely, but for a sequence limit they are invisible.

🎯 EXAM TIP
To answer an ε–N question, solve the inequality |aₙ − L| < ε for n and take N to be the threshold. Then check the boundary case — questions here are usually built on whether n = N itself is included, and the definition says n > N with a strict less than ε.
"}, "RANALYSIS/ch1/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Two powerful convergence tools that don't require knowing the limit in advance: monotone + bounded ⇒ convergent, and Cauchy ⇒ convergent (in ℝ). Both are consequences of completeness.

Monotone Convergence Theorem
A sequence that is monotone (always increasing or always decreasing) and bounded converges — to its sup (if increasing) or inf (if decreasing).
Cauchy sequence
(aₙ) is Cauchy if for every ε>0 there is N with |aₘ − aₙ| < ε for all m,n > N. In ℝ, a sequence converges iff it is Cauchy.
WORKED EXAMPLE — monotone convergence

Let a₁ = 1, aₙ₊₁ = √(2 + aₙ). One shows (by induction) the sequence is increasing and bounded above by 2.

By the Monotone Convergence Theorem it converges to some L, and L = √(2 + L) ⇒ L² − L − 2 = 0 ⇒ L = 2.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

'Cauchy ⇒ convergent' is special to COMPLETE spaces like ℝ. In ℚ a Cauchy sequence can fail to converge (e.g. rational approximations to √2).

📊 FIGURE — Bounded + increasing = convergent
The staircase climbs but can never pass its ceiling — completeness forces it to pile up against the supremum and converge there. This is the Monotone Convergence Theorem, and the same picture explains why Cauchy sequences (terms crowding together) must converge in ℝ.
📊 FIGURE — the standard three-step argument
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The Babylonian iteration converges to √2

Let a₁ = 2 and aₙ₊₁ = (aₙ + 2/aₙ)/2. The sequence decreases and stays above 0, so by the Monotone Convergence Theorem it converges to some L. Because it converges, aₙ₊₁ and aₙ share that limit, so letting n → ∞ in the recurrence:

L = (L + 2/L)/2  ⟹  2L = L + 2/L  ⟹  L = 2/L  ⟹  L² = 2

The terms are all positive, so L = √2 ≈ 1.41421 rather than −√2.

Numerically: 2, 1.5, 1.41667, 1.414216, 1.4142136 — five terms for seven correct digits. This is Newton's method applied to x² − 2, which is why it is so fast.

Note the logic: you may only pass to the limit in the recurrence after establishing that the limit exists. Solving L = (L + 2/L)/2 first would be assuming what has to be proved.

🎯 EXAM TIP
The monotone convergence theorem is what lets you find a limit you cannot write in closed form: prove monotone, prove bounded, conclude the limit exists, and only then substitute L into the recurrence. Sign or positivity of the terms is usually what picks the correct root at the end.
"}, "RANALYSIS/ch2/s1": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The ε–δ definition is the rigorous heart of calculus: continuity means small input changes force small output changes, made precise with quantifiers.

Continuity at a point
f is continuous at a if for every ε>0 there is δ>0 such that |x − a| < δ implies |f(x) − f(a)| < ε. Equivalently, lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a).
WORKED EXAMPLE — ε–δ proof

Show f(x) = 3x is continuous at a = 2.

Given ε>0, want |3x − 6| < ε, i.e. 3|x − 2| < ε, i.e. |x − 2| < ε/3.

Choose δ = ε/3. Then |x−2| < δ ⇒ |3x − 6| = 3|x−2| < 3·(ε/3) = ε. ∎

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

δ is chosen AFTER ε and generally depends on ε (and often on the point a). The logic is 'for all ε, there exists δ'.

📊 FIGURE — The ε–δ game, drawn as boxes
The challenge: an ε-band around f(a) (amber). The response: a δ-window around a (indigo) whose image lands entirely inside the band. Continuity at a = every ε challenge has a winning δ. Steeper functions demand smaller δ for the same ε.
📊 FIGURE — three ways to say the same thing
🎯 EXAM TIP
Continuity at a is equivalent to lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a). That single equation quietly asserts three things — f(a) exists, the limit exists, and they agree — and each of the three standard discontinuities is one of them failing. The sequential form is usually the easiest way to disprove continuity: find one sequence xₙ → a whose images do not tend to f(a).
"}, "RANALYSIS/ch2/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

On a closed bounded interval, continuity yields strong guarantees: it hits every intermediate value (IVT), attains a max and min (EVT), and is even uniformly continuous. These follow from completeness/compactness.

IVT & EVT
IVT: a continuous f on [a,b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b). EVT: a continuous f on [a,b] attains a maximum and a minimum.
Uniform continuity
f is uniformly continuous if one δ works for all points simultaneously (δ depends on ε only, not on x). A continuous function on a closed bounded interval is automatically uniformly continuous.
WORKED EXAMPLE — using the IVT

Show x³ + x − 1 = 0 has a root in [0,1].

f(0) = −1 < 0 and f(1) = 1 > 0. f is continuous, so by the IVT it takes the value 0 somewhere in (0,1). ∎

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

EVT and 'continuous ⇒ uniformly continuous' require a CLOSED and BOUNDED interval. On (0,1), f(x)=1/x is continuous but unbounded and not uniformly continuous.

📊 FIGURE — The Intermediate Value Theorem
A continuous curve from below the level N to above it MUST cross N somewhere — continuity forbids jumping over values. This is how you prove equations have roots: f(1) < 0 < f(2) forces a zero in between.
📊 FIGURE — where the quantifiers sit
🎯 EXAM TIP
1/x on (0, 1) is continuous but not uniformly continuous, because it blows up near 0 — no single δ works for the whole interval. The difference is purely where the quantifier sits: ordinary continuity lets δ depend on the point, uniform continuity does not. Note the rescue: on a closed bounded interval every continuous function is automatically uniformly continuous, so the open endpoint at 0 is what makes this example possible.
"}, "RANALYSIS/ch2/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The Mean Value Theorem is the workhorse of rigorous calculus: it converts local (derivative) information into global (function) conclusions — monotonicity, bounds, and Taylor's theorem all flow from it.

Derivative
f'(a) = lim_{h→0} [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h, when the limit exists. Differentiable ⇒ continuous (but not conversely, e.g. |x| at 0).
Mean Value Theorem
If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), there exists c ∈ (a,b) with f'(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a).
WORKED EXAMPLE — MVT consequence

If f'(x) = 0 for all x on an interval, then f is constant.

For any two points, MVT gives f(b) − f(a) = f'(c)(b − a) = 0, so f(b) = f(a). ∎

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Differentiability implies continuity, but NOT vice versa. |x| is continuous everywhere yet not differentiable at 0 (the corner).

📊 FIGURE — The Mean Value Theorem
The dashed secant’s slope is the AVERAGE rate over [a, b]. The MVT promises a point c where the tangent (green) is parallel to it — the instantaneous rate equals the average rate somewhere. If you averaged 60 mph, at some instant you were doing exactly 60.
📊 FIGURE — one theorem, two forms
🎯 EXAM TIP
Rolle's theorem is the MVT special case where f(a) = f(b). Equal endpoint values make the secant slope zero, so the guaranteed point has f′(c) = 0. Watch the hypotheses in exam questions: continuity is required on the closed interval but differentiability only on the open one — which is why |x| on [−1, 1] is not a counterexample to Rolle, it simply fails the differentiability hypothesis.
"}, "RANALYSIS/ch3/s1": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The Riemann integral defines area rigorously via upper and lower sums squeezing together. Understanding when a function IS integrable (and when it isn't) is a core analysis skill.

Riemann integrability
Using partitions, form upper sums U(f,P) and lower sums L(f,P). f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] if inf U = sup L; that common value is ∫ₐᵇ f. Continuous functions (and bounded functions with finitely many discontinuities) are integrable.
Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
If f is continuous and F' = f, then ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a); and d/dx ∫ₐˣ f(t)dt = f(x). It links the two halves of calculus.
WORKED EXAMPLE — a non-integrable function

The Dirichlet function (1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals) on [0,1]:

Every subinterval contains both rationals and irrationals, so every upper sum = 1 and every lower sum = 0. inf U = 1 ≠ 0 = sup L, so it is NOT Riemann integrable.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Riemann integrability requires upper and lower sums to converge to the SAME value. Too many discontinuities (like Dirichlet's everywhere) break this.

📊 FIGURE — Upper and lower Riemann sums squeezing the area
On each strip, the lower sum uses the infimum (dark bars) and the upper sum the supremum (light caps). Integrability means refining the partition drives the two totals together; their common limit is the integral.
📊 FIGURE — differentiating an integral, and integrating a jump
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — d/dx of an integral whose upper limit is x²

Write F(u) = ∫₁ᵘ eᵗ dt, so the quantity is F(x²). By the chain rule and FTC part 1:

d/dx F(x²) = F′(x²)·2x = e^(x²)·2x = 2x·e^(x²)

Check it directly: ∫₁^{x²} eᵗ dt = e^(x²) − e, whose derivative is 2x·e^(x²) — the constant e differentiates away. Both routes agree.

The step people miss is the factor g′(x) = 2x. Without the chain rule you would write e^(x²), which is wrong by exactly that factor.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Integrating a function with a jump

Let f(x) = 1 on [0, 1) and f(x) = 2 on [1, 2]. The function is bounded and has a single discontinuity, so it is Riemann integrable — integrability does not require continuity, only that the discontinuities be small enough (here, one point).

∫₀² f = (1)(1) + (2)(1) = 3

The value at the single jump point is irrelevant: changing f at finitely many points never changes the integral.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Two habits for this section. When the limit of integration is a function of x, the answer always carries the factor g′(x). And when a question asks whether a jump function is integrable, the answer is yes — a bounded function with finitely many discontinuities is Riemann integrable, and its integral is just the sum of the rectangles.
"}, "RANALYSIS/ch3/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Infinite series underlie power series, Fourier analysis, and numerical methods. The convergence tests decide whether an infinite sum has a finite value.

Convergence
Σaₙ converges if its partial sums sₙ = a₁+...+aₙ converge. Necessary (not sufficient): aₙ → 0. Absolute convergence (Σ|aₙ| converges) ⇒ convergence.
Key tests
Geometric Σrⁿ converges iff |r|<1. p-series Σ1/nᵖ converges iff p>1. Ratio test: lim|aₙ₊₁/aₙ| < 1 ⇒ converges. Alternating series with terms decreasing to 0 converge.
WORKED EXAMPLE — harmonic vs alternating harmonic

Σ1/n (harmonic) DIVERGES (p=1, not >1) even though 1/n → 0.

Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n (alternating harmonic) CONVERGES by the alternating series test — but only conditionally, since Σ1/n diverges.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

aₙ → 0 is necessary but NOT sufficient: the harmonic series has terms → 0 yet diverges. And conditional convergence (converges but not absolutely) can be reordered to any sum.

📊 FIGURE — Harmonic (p = 1) creeps to infinity; p = 2 levels off
Both series have terms shrinking to zero — but the harmonic partial sums keep climbing without bound (diverges), while Σ1/n² flattens out below 2 (converges to π²/6). This is the p-series rule in one picture: p ≤ 1 diverges, p > 1 converges.
📊 FIGURE — the tool for Σ n xⁿ
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Evaluating Σ n/2ⁿ

First establish convergence with the ratio test: aₙ₊₁/aₙ = ((n+1)/2ⁿ⁺¹)·(2ⁿ/n) = (n+1)/(2n) → 1/2 < 1, so the series converges absolutely.

Then use the identity Σ_{n≥1} n xⁿ = x/(1 − x)², obtained by differentiating the geometric series term by term and multiplying by x. With x = 1/2:

Σ n/2ⁿ = (1/2)/(1 − 1/2)² = (1/2)/(1/4) = 2

A partial-sum sanity check: 0.5, 1.0, 1.375, 1.625, 1.78125, … climbing toward 2. The terms n/2ⁿ eventually shrink because the exponential in the denominator outruns the linear numerator.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Σ_{n=1}^∞ n/2ⁿ = 2. The general tool is worth memorising: differentiating the geometric series gives Σ n xⁿ = x/(1 − x)² for |x| < 1. Any series of the form (polynomial in n)·xⁿ converges for |x| < 1 — the exponential always wins — and this differentiation trick is how you get the exact value.
"}, "RANALYSIS/ch3/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

When does a limit of continuous functions stay continuous, or an integral pass to the limit? The answer is uniform convergence — a subtlety that pointwise limits miss.

Pointwise vs uniform
fₙ → f pointwise if fₙ(x) → f(x) for each fixed x. Uniform convergence is stronger: one N works for ALL x at once (sup|fₙ − f| → 0).
What uniform convergence preserves
A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, and ∫fₙ → ∫f. Pointwise limits can destroy continuity and swap limit/integral incorrectly.
WORKED EXAMPLE — pointwise loses continuity

fₙ(x) = xⁿ on [0,1] converges pointwise to f(x) = 0 for x<1 and f(1) = 1 — a DISCONTINUOUS limit.

So the convergence is NOT uniform (each fₙ is continuous, but the limit isn't).

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Pointwise convergence does not preserve continuity, integrals, or derivatives. You need UNIFORM convergence to interchange the limit with continuity/integration safely.

📊 FIGURE — Uniform convergence: the whole function inside an ε-tube
Draw a tube of radius ε around the limit f. Uniform convergence demands that beyond some N, EVERY fₙ lies entirely inside the tube — the worst point obeys. Pointwise convergence lets different x settle at different speeds, which is exactly how continuity can break.
📊 FIGURE — uniformity is about the worst point
🎯 EXAM TIP
On ℝ, fₙ(x) = x/n converges pointwise to 0 but not uniformly, because sup_{x∈ℝ}|x/n| is infinite for every n. The test to apply is always the same: compute the supremum of the error over the whole domain and ask whether that tends to 0. The same formula is uniformly convergent on [0, 1] — so uniformity is a property of the function and its domain, never the formula alone.
"}, "RANALYSIS/solving/sv1": {"body": "

Formulas & method

For a rational sequence a_n = p(n)/q(n), divide top and bottom by the highest power of n: the limit equals the ratio of leading coefficients when degrees match, 0 when the bottom wins, and ±∞ when the top wins.

Useful standard limits

  • n^(1/n) → 1, (1 + 1/n)^n → e
  • 2^n / n! → 0 (factorial beats exponential)
  • Conjugate trick: √(n²+n) − n = n / (√(n²+n) + n) → 1/2

Sup / inf of a set

The supremum is the least upper bound, the infimum the greatest lower bound — neither need belong to the set. For {1/n : n ∈ ℕ} the values are 1, 1/2, 1/3, … so sup = 1 (attained) and inf = 0 (a limit, not attained).

Recursive limits

If a_(n+1) = g(a_n) converges to L, then L = g(L). For a_(n+1) = √(2 + a_n): solve L = √(2+L) ⇒ L² − L − 2 = 0 ⇒ L = 2.

ε–N definition

To find the smallest N with |a_n − L| < ε for all n ≥ N, solve the inequality for n and round up. Example: 1/n < 0.01 ⇒ n > 100 ⇒ smallest N = 101.

"}, "RANALYSIS/solving/sv2": {"body": "

Formulas & method

Geometric & telescoping series

For |r| < 1, Σ_(n=0)^∞ r^n = 1/(1 − r). Telescoping: Σ 1/(n(n+1)) = Σ (1/n − 1/(n+1)) = 1.

Radius of convergence

For Σ a_n x^n, R = 1 / limsup |a_n|^(1/n). If a_n = 1/3^n then |a_n|^(1/n) = 1/3 so R = 3.

Limits testing continuity

A function is continuous at c when lim_(x→c) f(x) = f(c). Factor to remove a hole: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = x + 2 → 4 as x → 2. Standard: lim_(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1.

Counting discontinuities

Factor numerator and denominator; each zero of the denominator (removable hole or pole) is a point of discontinuity. (x² − 1)/(x² − 3x + 2) = (x−1)(x+1)/((x−1)(x−2)) is discontinuous at x = 1 and x = 2 — 2 points.

Sup / inf and uniform convergence

On an interval, evaluate critical points and endpoints. For f(x) = x² on (−1, 2]: min at x = 0 gives inf 0, max at x = 2 gives sup 4. A sequence f_n → f converges uniformly iff sup_x |f_n(x) − f(x)| → 0. For f_n(x) = x^n on [0,1] this sup equals 1 for every n, so convergence is only pointwise.

Formulas & method

For a rational sequence a_n = (p·n^k + ...)/(q·n^k + ...), divide top and bottom by the highest power n^k; the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients p/q. Lower-order terms vanish since 1/n → 0.

Recursive limits

If a_n → L and a_(n+1) = f(a_n) with f continuous, then L = f(L). Solve that equation for L (rejecting values outside the sequence's range). Example: a_(n+1) = √(2 + a_n) gives L = √(2 + L), so L^2 - L - 2 = 0, (L-2)(L+1) = 0, hence L = 2.

ε-N estimates

To find the smallest N with |a_n - L| less than ε for all n ≥ N, solve the inequality for n. For a_n = 1/n and L = 0: 1/n less than ε means n greater than 1/ε, so N is the first integer past 1/ε.

Sup and inf

The supremum is the least upper bound and the infimum the greatest lower bound; neither need belong to the set. For {1/n : n ≥ 1} the values are 1, 1/2, 1/3, ..., so sup = 1 (attained) and inf = 0 (not attained).

Useful trick: for √(n^2 + n) - n, multiply by the conjugate to get n/(√(n^2+n) + n) → 1/2.

"}, "RANALYSIS/solving2/sv2": {"body": "

Formulas & method

A geometric series Σ (from n=0) r^n converges to 1/(1 - r) when |r| is less than 1. Starting the index at n = 1 gives r/(1 - r). A finite geometric sum is Σ (from n=0 to m) r^n = (r^(m+1) - 1)/(r - 1).

Telescoping

Write terms as differences: 1/(n(n+1)) = 1/n - 1/(n+1), so the partial sum collapses to 1 - 1/(N+1) → 1.

Radius of convergence

For Σ c_n x^n use the ratio test: R = lim |c_n / c_(n+1)|. For Σ x^n / n! the factorials give R = ∞; for Σ x^n / 2^n the ratio |x|/2 less than 1 gives R = 2.

Continuity via limits

A removable gap like (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) simplifies to x + 1 for x ≠ 1, so the value making it continuous at x = 1 is 2. A rational function is discontinuous exactly where its denominator is zero — count those roots.

For sup/inf of a continuous function on an interval, evaluate at endpoints and interior critical points; a downward parabola's vertex gives a max, an upward one gives a min.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

\n
THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its \"J-Method\"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
\n
THE 3-STEP LOOP
\n\n\n\n
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
\n
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
\n\n\n\n\n
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
\nStart the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
\n
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
\n
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
\n
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers \"learn it in 25 minutes\" instead of hours.

▸ Derivative f'(a) = lim_{h→0} [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h, when the limit exists. Differentiable ⇒ continuous (but not conversely, e.g. |x| at 0).

▸ Mean Value Theorem If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), there exists c ∈ (a,b) with f'(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a).
